reference.source: Standard endocrinology texts and diabetes insipidus guidance
clinicalPearls: Presents with polyuria and polydipsia due to deficient secretion of arginine vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone)
Most familial cases are autosomal dominant, caused by mutations in the AVP gene, with symptoms often appearing in early childhood rather than at birth
Symptoms may be progressive over years as vasopressin-producing neurones are gradually lost
A family history spanning generations distinguishes it from acquired causes such as tumour, trauma, or infiltration
The condition is now often termed arginine vasopressin deficiency to reduce confusion with diabetes mellitus
Diagnosis uses a water deprivation test with response to desmopressin, increasingly supported by copeptin measurement
Treatment is with desmopressin replacement, with attention to avoiding water intoxication from overtreatment
reference.pathophysiology: Familial central diabetes insipidus arises from mutations in the AVP gene, which encodes the precursor of arginine vasopressin. Most mutations produce a misfolded precursor that accumulates and is thought to be cytotoxic to the magnocellular neurones of the hypothalamus that synthesise the hormone. Progressive loss of these neurones reduces vasopressin secretion from the posterior pituitary, so the kidney cannot concentrate urine; large volumes of dilute urine are produced and compensatory thirst drives high fluid intake. The gradual neuronal loss explains the typical delayed and progressive onset.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired central diabetes insipidus from tumour, surgery, or trauma
Infiltrative disease such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis or sarcoidosis
Wolfram syndrome as part of a wider genetic disorder
additionalInvestigations: Paired serum and urine osmolality measurements
Water deprivation test with desmopressin challenge
Copeptin measurement, including stimulated testing where available
AVP gene testing and family screening
Pituitary magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural or infiltrative causes
Serum sodium, glucose, and renal function
redFlags: Hypernatraemia and dehydration when access to water is limited
Severe symptoms in infancy with poor feeding and failure to thrive
Features suggesting a structural pituitary lesion rather than familial disease
Hyponatraemia from excessive desmopressin or overhydration
reference.prognosis: With reliable desmopressin replacement and free access to water, prognosis is excellent and normal life is expected; the main risks come from dehydration when fluid intake is restricted and from hyponatraemia due to overtreatment.
pitfalls: Confusing the condition with diabetes mellitus because of the shared name
Missing the gradual, progressive childhood onset and attributing symptoms to behaviour
Overtreating with desmopressin and precipitating hyponatraemia
Failing to distinguish central from nephrogenic or psychogenic causes before treatment
references: Endocrine society and specialist guidance on diabetes insipidus / arginine vasopressin deficiency
management: Desmopressin replacement as the mainstay to restore urinary concentrating ability
Ensure free access to water with thirst-guided fluid intake to prevent dehydration
Titrate desmopressin against serum sodium to avoid dilutional hyponatraemia from overtreatment
Patient and family education on sick-day management, recognising dehydration and avoiding water intoxication
Careful fluid and electrolyte management during intercurrent illness, surgery or whenever thirst or access to water is impaired
Genetic counselling with AVP gene testing and family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance
Endocrinology follow-up with periodic review of the desmopressin regimen
